issues.legal_issue: The governance of a public shrine of composite character is not determined by Hindu or Muhammadan personal law, and an unpleaded or indefinite custom cannot establish its governing rules.
material_facts: The shrine contained the tombs of a Muslim saint and a Hindu princess, and people of different faiths made offerings there.
Its management had involved people of different faiths, but no definite custom governing the selection or rights of managers was pleaded or established.
issues.conclusion: Neither Hindu nor Muhammadan law governed the shrine, and the alleged custom could not be relied on; its governance was to be determined under the general law of public religious and charitable trusts.
issues.legal_principle: Where an institution does not fall within either relevant personal-law system, its governance must rest on a proved special custom or the general law of public religious and charitable trusts. A vague allegation of family management, without a definite custom, does not establish the governing rule. No earlier cases were relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.public_composite_shrine: The institution served the public and combined religious or burial associations of more than one faith.
predicates.no_definite_custom_pleaded_or_proved: The party asserting a customary rule did not plead or establish a definite rule governing management.

issues.definition: When a public shrine has composite character and no definite custom governing its management is established, its governance is determined under the general law applicable to public trusts.

issues.legal_issue: A de facto manager may recover or collect offerings for a public institution’s benefit in the ordinary course of management, but that status alone does not establish a right to manage indefinitely or to treat the offerings as personal property.
material_facts: The plaintiffs and their family had been in de facto management, but their claim to hereditary management was not established.
The defendant had been present in a permissive capacity and had no independent rights; he claimed to collect offerings for the shrine’s upkeep and benefit, not as personal property.
The plaintiffs’ pre-suit notice asserted personal control over the income, and the second plaintiff’s evidence claimed any balance remaining after expenses.
The offerings had been attached during the dispute and deposited in the treasury, and a suit to settle the institution’s governance was contemplated.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to declare an indefinite right to manage or a personal right to the offerings. It ordered an interim arrangement under which offerings could be used only as necessary for expenses; if a scheme suit was brought within the specified interval, the offerings were to be dealt with under that scheme, and otherwise the second plaintiff could collect and receive them for the institution’s benefit until displaced by someone with better title or authority.
issues.legal_principle: A de facto manager or trustee de son tort may sue to recover property or money for the trust and its benefit in the ordinary course of management. That limited authority does not confer an indefinite right to manage without title or a personal entitlement to trust property. The Court also contemplated a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure to frame a scheme; Sections 145 and 147 of the Criminal Procedure Code explained the attachment and deposit of the offerings, not the plaintiffs’ substantive title. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: public_trust_institution and de_facto_manager and no_established_title_to_indefinite_management and offerings_claimed_for_personal_use

predicates.public_trust_institution: The institution served the public, and its property or offerings were held for institutional purposes.
predicates.de_facto_manager: A person had in fact managed the institution without an established legal title to that management.
predicates.no_established_title_to_indefinite_manag: The person had not proved a title authorizing management to continue indefinitely.
predicates.offerings_claimed_for_personal_use: The manager asserted a personal entitlement to offerings or to the balance after expenses.

issues.definition: If a public institution is managed in fact by someone without established title to manage indefinitely, and that person claims offerings personally, the offerings are administered for the institution’s benefit under a scheme or until a person with better authority displaces that manager.

issues.legal_issue: The legal representatives of a deceased manager who claimed no hereditary management right have no entitlement to offerings held for the institution.
material_facts: The defendant died while the appeal was pending.
He had claimed to be the manager but had not claimed hereditary rights.
His stated claim to collect offerings was for the upkeep and benefit of the shrine and related purposes.
issues.conclusion: The defendant’s legal representatives had no right to the offerings; his management rights, if any, did not survive him as hereditary rights.
issues.legal_principle: A claim to manage that is not hereditary does not pass to the deceased manager’s legal representatives. Offerings claimed for the benefit of a public institution must be held for the persons authorized to administer them for those purposes. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.proceeding_concerns_public_institution_o: The proceeding concerns offerings held for the use or benefit of a public institution.
predicates.manager_has_died: The person who claimed to manage the institution died during the proceeding.
predicates.manager_claimed_no_hereditary_right: The deceased manager did not assert a hereditary right to management.

issues.definition: When a manager dies without claiming hereditary management, the manager’s estate has no right to offerings held for a public institution.

issues.legal_issue: A declaration of indefinite management cannot be founded solely on de facto management when no title to that continuing right has been established.
material_facts: The plaintiffs had established de facto management over a period of time.
Their hereditary-management claim was not established, and the Court found no proven title entitling them to continue managing indefinitely.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to make a sweeping declaration that the second plaintiff was entitled to continue as manager indefinitely merely because he had been in de facto management.
issues.legal_principle: A de facto manager may act for the institution in the ordinary course and recover property for its benefit, but the fact of management alone does not establish a continuing right to manage without a vestige of title. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_declaration_of_continui: A party in a civil proceeding seeks a declaration that the party may continue managing an institution.
predicates.management_is_de_facto: The party’s management is shown by the fact of having managed the institution rather than by an established legal title.
predicates.no_title_to_continuing_management_is_est: The party has not established a legal basis for a continuing right to manage.

issues.definition: When a party seeks a continuing management declaration based only on de facto management and establishes no title to continue, the declaration is refused.

issues.legal_issue: A remand is unnecessary when an amendment merely formalizes relief supported by facts already pleaded and any needed response can be obtained without restarting proceedings.
material_facts: The plaintiffs had pleaded the facts on which relief for the institution’s benefit could be granted, although they had not sought that relief in proper form.

The High Court permitted an amendment clarifying that the suit was brought for the institution by its de facto managers, then set aside the trial decree and remanded the suit to allow a supplementary written statement.
The Supreme Court considered the amendment purely formal and said the High Court could have called for a reply and determined whether further proceedings were needed.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the remand because it was unnecessary; the High Court should have obtained any required reply itself and decided whether further proceedings were warranted.
issues.legal_principle: Where an amendment is formal and the facts supporting the properly framed relief are already pleaded, a remand is not required merely to allow a response; the appellate court can call for the response and determine whether further proceedings are necessary. No earlier cases or statutory provisions were relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_remand_in_civil_suit and amendment_is_formal and supporting_facts_are_already_pleaded and any_needed_reply_can_be_obtained_by_appellate_court

predicates.appeal_challenges_remand_in_civil_suit: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order that remanded a civil suit.
predicates.amendment_is_formal: The amendment changes the form or clarification of the claim rather than introducing a materially new factual basis.
predicates.supporting_facts_are_already_pleaded: The facts necessary to support the properly framed relief are already set out in the pleadings.
predicates.any_needed_reply_can_be_obtained_by_appe: The opposing party’s response to the amendment can be obtained and considered by the appellate court.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal challenges a remand, the amendment is formal, its factual basis is already pleaded, and any reply can be obtained by the appellate court, the remand is unnecessary and is set aside.
